title: Industrial Property Identification
name: Industrial Property Identification
metaTitle: Industrial Property Identification in San Jose, CA
metaDescription: Industrial property identification for San Jose 1031 exchangers, screening North San Jose and Golden Triangle candidates against real seller intent.

sections.html: Industrial replacement candidates in San Jose are concentrated in a handful of corridors, North San Jose and the Golden Triangle chief among them, and land scarcity across the valley means the realistic pool an exchanger can identify from is smaller than the zoning map suggests. We've spent years tracking which buildings in this stock actually trade versus which ones just look available, and that distinction matters more here than in markets where inventory is easier to come by.

sections.heading: Where San Jose's Industrial Stock Actually Sits
sections.html: The bulk of tradeable industrial and flex product sits in North San Jose and the Golden Triangle, bounded roughly by Highway 101, 880, and 237, with a secondary pocket further south around Edenvale and the Monterey Road corridor. Newer construction skews toward semiconductor and hardware R&D specs, while the older stock nearer Berryessa tends toward straightforward distribution and light manufacturing space with lower clear heights and smaller truck courts. Knowing which pocket a candidate sits in tells us most of what to expect on power capacity and clear height before we've even pulled the listing details.

sections.heading: Why Zoning Maps Overstate the Real Pool
sections.html: A parcel zoned for industrial use isn't automatically a candidate; land scarcity across the valley means a meaningful share of zoned industrial land is already built out, under long-term ground leases, or held by owner-occupants with no intention of selling in the near term. We cross-check zoning against actual ownership history and recent transaction activity before adding a building to an identification list, rather than treating a zoning designation as evidence of real availability.

sections.heading: What We Screen For Before a Building Goes on the List
sections.html:
Before an industrial candidate makes it onto a 45-day identification letter, we confirm a specific set of details that go well beyond confirming the building is simply for sale. That includes:

  • Actual seller intent versus a speculative or test listing
  • Clear height, loading configuration, and power capacity against the buyer's use
  • Any pending seismic retrofit obligations tied to the building's age
  • Environmental history, particularly on older industrial parcels with prior manufacturing use
  • Realistic closing timeline given the seller's own circumstances

Any one of these can disqualify an otherwise attractive candidate, which is why we run through the full list before a building goes on the letter rather than after.

sections.heading: Older Buildings Converting to Flex or Lab Use
sections.html: A number of older industrial buildings in the Golden Triangle and along North First Street have been repositioned toward flex or lab-adjacent use as demand shifted, which changes both the pricing and the diligence needed on a candidate. A building marketed as industrial but recently upgraded with lab infrastructure, higher-capacity electrical, or reinforced floor loads carries different power, water, and permitting considerations than a straightforward distribution building, and we treat these as a distinct screening category rather than lumping them in with traditional industrial stock. Pricing on these converted buildings can run well ahead of nearby straightforward distribution space, which surprises owners comparing against older per-square-foot expectations for the same corridor.

sections.heading: Timing an Industrial Search Against the 45-Day Window
sections.html:
Because the realistic pool of tradeable industrial buildings in this market is genuinely thin, we start the search as soon as an owner signals intent to exchange, well before the relinquished property is under contract, so the 45-day letter reflects buildings that have already been vetted rather than a rushed list assembled under deadline pressure. A short list built in week one of a 45-day window, with no prior screening, is the single biggest risk factor we see in industrial exchanges here.

Owners who engage us early enough often end up with a shortlist that's already been walked, priced, and checked against seller intent well before the relinquished property even goes to market, which changes the entire tone of the 45-day window from reactive to routine.

faqs.q: How much industrial inventory actually trades in San Jose in a given year?
faqs.a: It varies with the cycle, but land scarcity keeps the pool tight compared to markets with more available greenfield land. We don't quote specific figures without pulling current data, but the practical effect is that early, thorough screening matters more here than in looser markets, since a thin quarter can leave very few genuine candidates to choose from.

faqs.q: Does a building's zoning guarantee it's a real candidate?
faqs.a: No. Zoning only confirms permitted use, not seller intent or actual availability. We check ownership history and recent activity before treating any zoned parcel as a genuine identification candidate, since a for-sale sign is a starting point, not confirmation of anything.

faqs.q: What's different about buildings converted to flex or lab use?
faqs.a: They typically carry upgraded electrical, water, and floor load capacity beyond standard industrial spec, which changes both pricing and the diligence checklist compared to a straightforward distribution building.

faqs.q: Do older industrial buildings need seismic retrofit review before identification?
faqs.a: Often yes, particularly unreinforced masonry or soft-story construction. We flag any pending retrofit obligation before a building goes on the identification list so it isn't a surprise during financing.

faqs.q: When should an industrial replacement search start relative to selling the relinquished property?
faqs.a: As early as possible, ideally before the relinquished property is even listed, given how thin this market's tradeable industrial inventory can run in any given window. Owners who wait until after listing are often working from whatever is left over rather than a genuinely screened field of candidates.
